newsitem.title: UK: "Boom-bust" or tax hikes if UK joins EMU - report.
newsitem.headline: "Boom-bust" or tax hikes if UK joins EMU - report.

text.p: Britain will face either a "boom-bust" economy, or a tax rise if it joins European Monetary Union on January 1, 1999, according to research published by independent research organisation, Oxford Economic Forecasting on Monday.

Using its own economic model of the world economy, OEF compared EMU entry against a base forecast if the UK remained outside of EMU and found that GDP growth could initially get a boost of almost one percent as interest rates fell to continental levels.

"These pressures would in turn provoke a sharp downturn in growth as higher domestic inflation led to a marked loss of competitiveness, which could not be alleviated by a lower exchange rate in a monetary union," said Adrian Cooper and John Gaster, authors of the report.
They forecast growth would slow to 1.4 percent in 2002, sinking to 0.7 percent in 2004 as the UK lost its competitiveness.

To soften the inflationary impact, OEF reckon that the basic tax rate would have to rise to 28 pence in the pound and be sustained at that level for at least two years. The current basic rate is 24 pence.
Stringent fiscal measures would put a lid on inflation, keeping it at 3.6 and 3.4 percent in 1999 and 2000, while growth would be steadier, at 2.5 percent in 1999, dipping to 1.5 percent in 2002.
The UK has an inflation target band of one to four percent, reaching 2.5 percent by the end of this Paliament.

In a recent Reuter poll, only six percent of respondents thought the UK would join EMU in the first round, but if it did, the economic effects would probably lie between the two scenarios Cooper, Director of Forecasting at OEF told Reuters.
"It would be a very brave Government who would raise taxes by the amount necessary at the 1998 Budget," he said. "It's quite possible that fiscal policy would not be tightened substantially enough."
Cooper also warned that the same scenarios could quite easily apply to the other peripheral countries such as Italy.
